title: Python syntax bridge

story: Every night Nova, our agent that turns a Jira ticket into a pull request, practises on a few old tickets whose real fixes we already know, and a short Python script turns the results into one number: how many attempts passed. Each attempt writes a 1 or a 0 into a text file, and the script reads the file and divides. Yesterday the number was 60%. This morning it is 0%, although the file still holds three 1s and two 0s, and nothing crashed.

The script looks almost like TypeScript. One function says it takes list[int]. A teammate changed the function that reads the file, and it now says it returns list[str]. In TypeScript the build would stop right there, on that line. In Python the script ran, compared the text "1" with the number 1, found them different every time, and printed 0% without a single warning.
hook.question: Python looks so much like TypeScript. Where does it really behave differently, and if the language does not check the types, what does?

p: Start with the good news: almost everything you know from TypeScript still applies in Python, and mostly the punctuation changes. Here is the script from the story. Read it as if it were TypeScript, and use the notes only on the lines that look strange.

Three rules explain most of the strangeness. A block starts with a colon and is made of the indented lines below it, so there are no braces, and the indentation is not style but syntax. A function is def, its parameter types follow a colon as in TypeScript, and its return type follows an arrow, ->. And Python has one empty value, None, where TypeScript has both null and undefined, which is why reading a missing key from a dict (Python's plain object) raises a KeyError instead of quietly giving undefined. Names use snake_case for functions and variables and PascalCase for classes; fcp's formatter, black, keeps the rest consistent.

notes.text: The module comes first, then what you take from it: import { Path } from "pathlib". pathlib is part of Python itself, so nothing is installed.
def is function. list[str] is string[]. The colon at the end opens the block.
split() with no argument splits on spaces and line breaks, so every line of the file becomes one string.
A list comprehension: rewards.filter(r => r === 1) written as one expression. == compares values like ===; Python has no loose ==, so "1" == 1 is False.
len(x) is x.length. / always gives a decimal number; // is division that drops the remainder.
No let or const: assigning to a name creates it.
An f-string is a template literal: {expr} is ${expr}. :.0% prints 0.6 as 60%.

p: Python has async and await too, with one difference that surprises every TypeScript developer. Calling an async def function does not start it. It returns a coroutine, an object that does nothing until something awaits it, and a script has no top-level await. So a script starts the event loop itself with asyncio.run(main()), and asyncio.gather(a(), b()) plays the part of Promise.all.

If you call main() without asyncio.run, nothing runs, and Python only prints RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'main' was never awaited. Most of fcp's backend is synchronous, because Django views and Celery tasks (jobs that the backend's background workers run) are plain def functions, so you meet async mainly in scripts that call several services at once.

read.h: Types are hints, and nothing checks them when the code runs
p: Back to the 0%. read_rewards promised a list of strings, pass_rate asked for a list of numbers, and Python handed one to the other without a word. This is the biggest difference from TypeScript. In Python the type after a colon or an arrow is called a type hint (or annotation). Python stores it and then ignores it when the code runs, so nothing ever compares the hint with the real value.

TypeScript has a compiler, tsc, that reads the types before anything runs and refuses to build when they disagree. Python has the same kind of tool, called a type checker, but it is a separate program that a project chooses to run. mypy and pyright are the common ones. Run mypy on the script and it finds the bug in a second, on the line where the strings are passed in:

Whether anyone runs a type checker is a decision each project makes. fcp's backend does not run one in CI. Its lint is black and isort for formatting, plus flake8 limited to real errors such as a name that does not exist or an import nobody uses. So in fcp the hints are documentation for people and agents, and the tests are what catch a wrong type. When you review Python, read every hint as a claim, and look for a test that would fail if the claim were false.
read.see:
$ uv run mypy score.py
score.py:14: error: Argument 1 to "pass_rate" has incompatible type "list[str]"; expected "list[int]"  [arg-type]
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)

read.h: A dataclass is an interface you can create
p: In TypeScript you would describe one attempt with an interface, { task: string; reward: number }, which disappears when the code runs. Python's closest match is a dataclass. You list the fields with their types, and the @dataclass line above the class (a decorator: a function that wraps the class below it) writes the constructor, a readable printout and == for you. Unlike an interface, a dataclass exists at run time. You create one with Trial(task="fe-bug-1", reward=1) and read t.reward with a dot.

A dataclass follows the same rule as everything else, though: its types are hints. Trial(task="fe-bug-1", reward="1") is created without complaint. So the value has to be converted where it enters the program, which is what int(reward) does below. When you want the check to happen automatically, there is Pydantic, a library that validates data at run time the way zod does. fcp's Python SDK is built on it, while scripts and tests mostly use plain dataclasses.

notes.text: frozen=True makes the fields read-only, like Readonly<Trial>.
A field is a name and a type hint. Fields with a default value must come after fields without one.
Unpacking: the two parts of the line go into two names, like const [task, reward] = line.split(" ").
Keyword arguments name each field, much like passing an object literal. int("1") is Number("1"), except int("one") raises a ValueError instead of giving NaN.

read.see:
$ uv run python trials.py
Trial(task='fe-bug-1', reward=1)
pass rate: 60%

deeper.h: Go deeper: the default value that is shared
p: In TypeScript, function f(seen: string[] = []) makes a new empty array on every call. In Python the default value is created once, when the def line runs, and every call shares that same object. So a list default that the function changes keeps growing from one call to the next, and no type checker notices, because the types are fine.

The usual fix is a None default, seen: list[str] | None = None, and seen = [] inside the function when it is None. Dataclasses protect you from the same trap: a list default on a field is an error, and you write field(default_factory=list) instead, which builds a new list for every object.

read.h: Where the code runs: pyproject.toml, .venv and uv
p: The last difference is where Python finds installed packages. In a Node project, package.json lists what you need, npm puts it in node_modules, and the lockfile pins exact versions. Python keeps installed packages in a virtual environment, a folder usually called .venv that holds a link to one Python interpreter and every package the project installed. Each project gets its own, so two projects never fight over versions. You can think of it as node_modules with its own copy of Node inside.

fcp manages all of this with uv, a tool that maps almost one to one onto npm. pyproject.toml is package.json, with one extra line, requires-python, for the Python version the project needs; fcp's backend asks for 3.13. uv.lock is package-lock.json. uv add --dev mypy is npm install -D mypy. uv sync --frozen installs exactly what uv.lock says and never rewrites it, which is what fcp's CI and Dockerfiles run. uv run <command> runs a command with the project's .venv, the way npm run finds tools in node_modules/.bin, and uvx <tool> runs a tool once without adding it, like npx.

This gives the most common Python error a simple explanation. If you type python3 instead of uv run python, you get your laptop's own Python, which cannot see the packages in .venv, and the import fails with ModuleNotFoundError. The fix is to run through uv run, not to install the package globally.

notes.text: The Python version is part of the project. uv downloads a matching Python if your laptop has none.
Run-time dependencies, like dependencies in package.json. uv add writes here.
Named groups of extra packages, like devDependencies but you can have several. fcp's cloud has groups such as dev, lint and test.
A range. The exact version lives in uv.lock, which you commit.

read.see:
$ python3 -c "import mypy"
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mypy'
$ uv run python -c "import mypy; print('found in .venv')"
found in .venv

deeper.h: Go deeper: an import is a path
p: A module is one .py file and a package is a folder of modules. An fcp import such as from rhinoCloud.rhinoCore.models.dataset import Dataset reads like a path: the file rhinoCloud/rhinoCore/models/dataset.py, and the class Dataset inside it. There is no bundler and no index file that collects exports; you import from the exact module.

Python looks for the first part of that path in a list of folders called sys.path: the folder of the script you run, any folders in the PYTHONPATH variable, and the packages in .venv. That is why fcp's cloud code runs from the cloud folder, and why a ModuleNotFoundError for one of our own modules usually means Python was started from the wrong folder.

lab.title: Catch the 0% bug
lab.goal: Reproduce the 0% pass rate, let a type checker find the wrong hint, and fix the script with a dataclass that converts the value where it enters.

guess.q: pass_rate is declared def pass_rate(rewards: list[int]) -> float, and the script passes it ["1", "0", "1", "1", "0"], a list of strings. What happens when you run it?

options.text: Python stops with a TypeError on the call, because the argument has the wrong type.
options.why: Python never compares a value with its type hint. The call goes through like any other.

options.text: It runs and prints pass rate: 0%, because "1" == 1 is never true.
options.why: The hint is only a note. The body compares each string with the number 1, finds no match, and divides 0 by 5.

options.text: It runs and prints pass rate: 60%, because Python converts "1" to 1 for you.
options.why: Python does not convert types on comparison. == between a string and a number is simply False, which is how the bug hides.

lab.build:
Change the input to one attempt per line with a task name and a reward: printf 'fe-bug-1 1
fe-bug-1 0
be-bug-7 1
be-bug-7 1
add-tests-3 0
' > trials.txt. Then write trials.py with a frozen dataclass Trial(task: str, reward: int), a function read_trials(path: Path) -> list[Trial] that converts the reward with int(), and pass_rate(trials: list[Trial]) -> float. Print the first Trial and the pass rate. Run it with uv run python trials.py, and check it with uv run mypy trials.py.
checks: uv run python score.py printed pass rate: 0% before any change.
uv run mypy score.py reported list[str] where list[int] was expected, on line 14.
python3 -c "import mypy" fails, and uv run python -c "import mypy" works.
uv run python trials.py prints Trial(task='fe-bug-1', reward=1) and pass rate: 60%.
uv run mypy trials.py prints Success: no issues found in 1 source file.
lab.fix: fix.py collects the tasks that failed. Run uv run python fix.py: on Monday it reports fe-bug-1, which is right, but on Tuesday every task passed and it still reports fe-bug-1. mypy finds nothing wrong, because the types are fine. Find why Tuesday remembers Monday (look at the default value of seen) and change the function so Tuesday prints an empty list.
explain: Why did score.py print 0% instead of stopping with an error, and which tool would have caught it before it ran?
fcp's backend runs no type checker in CI. What catches a wrong type there, and what do you look for when you review a Python function's hints?
Why can python3 not import mypy in the lab folder while uv run python can?
lab.done: trials.py prints pass rate: 60% with no mypy errors, and fix.py prints an empty list for Tuesday.

check.q: A function in an fcp pull request is declared def total_days(days: list[float]) -> float, and a new caller passes it a list of strings. CI is green. What does that tell you?

options.text: The caller must be fine, because Python would have refused the wrong type when the tests ran.
options.why: Python never checks a value against its hint while the code runs, so a green run proves nothing about the hint.

options.text: Nothing about the types: fcp runs no type checker, so only a test that uses the strings would fail.
options.why: fcp's lint checks formatting and real errors such as unknown names, not types. A test that exercises this caller is the only thing that would catch it.

options.text: flake8 would have reported the mismatch, so the hint must be wrong instead.
options.why: fcp runs flake8 with only its error rules, such as undefined names and unused imports. It does not compare types.

check.q: You write @dataclass class Trial: task: str; reward: int, and then call Trial(task="fe-bug-1", reward="1"). What happens?

options.text: A ValueError, because the dataclass checks each field's type.
options.why: A dataclass writes the constructor, the printout and ==, but it does not check types. That is what Pydantic adds.

options.text: Python converts "1" to the number 1, because the field says int.
options.why: Nothing converts the value. The object holds the string "1" until your own code calls int().

options.text: The object is created with reward set to the string "1".
options.why: The field type is a hint like any other. Convert at the edge, as int(reward) does, or use a validating library.

check.q: A teammate runs python3 manage.py test in fcp's cloud folder and gets ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django'. The project's uv.lock includes Django. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: They ran the laptop's own Python, which cannot see the packages in the project's .venv.
options.why: Packages live in the project's .venv. uv run python manage.py test (or the project's own commands) uses that environment.

options.text: uv.lock is out of date and Django must be added again with uv add django.
options.why: The lock already has Django. Adding it again changes nothing if the command still runs outside .venv.

options.text: Django must be installed globally with pip so every project can use it.
options.why: That is exactly what virtual environments avoid: each project keeps its own versions, and a global install hides the real problem.

p: Python appears in two places in our work. The fcp backend (the cloud service, the on-prem client and the SDK) is Python 3.13 managed with uv, formatted with black and isort, and checked by tests instead of a type checker, so the bug fixers, the upgrade fixer and the flaky-test fixer all change Python that you will review. And the eval bench in ai-agents/evals is a small uv project inside the TypeScript repo, because Harbor, the tool that runs the bench, is written in Python.
The bench's scoring script counts passes with sum(t["reward"] == 1 for t in trials), the same comparison as this lesson's story, which is why the rewards it reads must really be numbers.

tickets.why: mine.py is a plain Python script: regular expressions, subprocess calls to gh, and type hints like the ones in this lesson.
score.py compares each reward with 1 and computes pass rates; the 0% story is its failure mode.
poe doctor checks for uv, Python 3.13 and a cloud .venv that matches uv.lock, all explained here.
poe verify lints changed Python files with fcp's black, isort and flake8 setup.

words.plain: The type after a colon or an arrow in Python. Python stores it but never checks it when the code runs.
A separate tool, such as mypy or pyright, that reads the hints before the code runs, like tsc.
A class whose constructor, printout and == are written from its typed fields; the run-time cousin of an interface.
A project folder with a link to one Python and the project's installed packages, like node_modules with Node inside.
The tool that installs Python, creates .venv, adds packages and writes uv.lock; npm, nvm and npx in one.
The project file: name, Python version, dependencies and dependency groups; Python's package.json.

review.q: Translate this TypeScript into Python from memory: const passed = rewards.filter(r => r === 1).length;
review.a: passed = len([r for r in rewards if r == 1]). No const, a list comprehension for filter, len() for .length, and == for ===.

review.q: A teammate says "the hint says int, so I don't need int() when I read the file". What do you answer?
review.a: Hints are never checked at run time, so text from a file stays text. Convert where the data enters the program, or validate it with a library like Pydantic, and back it with a test.

review.q: Map these to npm: pyproject.toml, uv.lock, .venv, uv add --dev, uv sync --frozen, uv run, uvx.
review.a: package.json, package-lock.json, node_modules (with the interpreter), npm install -D, install exactly the lockfile like npm ci, npm run, npx.

remember: Python reads like TypeScript, but its types are hints nobody checks at run time, so convert data where it enters and let tests (or a type checker) prove the hints.
